articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO Live Updates: AI Firm Set to Begin Trading at $83 a Share Under ANT
articles.content_orig:
WHEN: Today, Thursday, November 19
Below is the unofficial transcript of CNBC's exclusive interview with Anthropic co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei today, Thursday, November 19, following the company's highly anticipated IPO. Following are links to video on CNBC.com: https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/19/anthropic-ceo-on-scaling-laws-i-dont-think-we-really-believed-it-until-it-actually-happened.html , https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/19/anthropics-debut-is-one-stop-on-the-journey-says-daniela-amodei.html , https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/19/dario-amodei-weare-hoping-to-be-investment-grade-in-the-future.html , https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/19/dario-amodei-on-if-jensen-huang-should-come-back-as-ceo-.html , and https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/19/anthropic-sibling-founders-reflect-on-ipo-journey.html .
All references must be sourced to CNBC.
ANDREW ROSS SORKIN: Hey, thanks, Carl. Big day here. And I am here with the co-founders of this company, brother and sister. It's an unbelievable story, Dario and Daniela Amodei. Thank you for being here. Congratulations on this big moment.
DANIELA AMODEI: Thank you for having us.
DARIO AMODEI: Thank you for having us.
SORKIN: Here's where I want to start this. When I first met you, you basically just practically started the company. And I'm so curious — you understood scaling laws at the beginning, perhaps better than anybody, but did you ever expect three, four, five years later here we would be and be talking about evaluation that starts with a T?
DARIO AMODEI: You know, the funny thing is, you look at the scaling laws and they're a line on a piece of paper, right? They predict that a model will have certain cognitive capabilities that will be capable of certain economic tasks. But it's one thing to kind of draw that line, and it's a totally different thing to see the consequences out in the world. And so I would say the scaling laws kind of imply that the technology and hopefully our work within it would — would have this scale. But I don't think we really believed it until it actually happened.
SORKIN: And it's happening right now. Daniela, this is now going to be the largest public benefit corporation to go public. What — for those folks who are watching this morning, even thinking about investing in the company, what does that mean, both for the company itself, but also the way investors should think about that?
DANIELA AMODEI: So, as a public benefit corporation, you know, part of why we decided to incorporate this way, is Anthropic mission is so much about how do we build something that is good for everybody? How do we really build for the public benefit? And part of what I think is so interesting about this structure is that we're actually legally required to balance shareholder interest with the public benefit, with the public good. And I think when Dario and I and our other co-founders were starting the organization, you know, we learned about this concept of a public benefit corporation. It really spoke to us, because we said, well, that's exactly what we're trying to do. We're really trying to do something that we do think can have this incredible economic value and impact, but we want it to be baked into essentially our structure that we also have to balance that against building things that are good for people.
SORKIN: OK, so here's the question. How do you balance the idea of growth and the idea of, for example, pacing at this point? This is something you have talked a lot about, pacing, given some of the safety concerns around AI? And how should the investor class think about those competing interests?
DARIO AMODEI: So, this, you know, this is one of the central tensions at the heart of the company. But it's really, because this technology is so powerful, it has so many effects in the world, it's something that every company in this space will have to face, whether they want to or not. We're just facing it more explicitly and more thoughtfully. And so, you think about something like pacing, the idea behind pacing was, you know, imagine that you have — you're driving your car at 60 miles an hour, and then you discover or invent something that could let you drive the car at 200 miles an hour, right? This is models building themselves, recursive self-improvement. What we have done with pacing is essentially said, look, you know, we could drive at 200 miles an hour. Maybe let's only drive at 90 miles an hour, spend time figuring out how to do that safely, and the rest of that surplus, we spend building the model in the right way. And you know, I think, in the long run, that will work out pretty well for the investors as well, because the company that builds the safest, that has trust of the customers and the enterprises of the world, I think that is the company that's going to be both best for society and, in the long run, I hope, best for the performance of the company. And I think that's what we often look for. We look for synergies, ways to make the two line up in the long run.
SORKIN:  What does success look like today? When we see the price of this, do you say to yourself, if this is up 10 percent, 20 percent, that's success? If it's up too much, is that not success? What does, I mean, you guys have spent a lot of time with your bankers and—
DARIO AMODEI:  I think that's one of the very few topics we're not allowed to talk about.
DANIELA AMODEI:  I think, you know, I think maybe the way I would put it is, Anthropic has always been a very long-term-focused company, right? We have always been thinking about, how is this technology going to be beneficial to people in the future, but also what can it do for people today? And so while today is a super exciting milestone and we're obviously really, really excited about it, I think it's, for us, it's like one stop on the journey, right? We think about this as, wow, this is an incredible moment for Anthropic, for our mission, but we're going to wake up tomorrow and we're going to be the same company. And I think that's really, at least for me, what I have been focusing on today.
SORKIN:  The rate of growth of this company has been extraordinary, but I want to understand the unlock and also understand the competition in the space, because, increasingly, you have open-weight models. You have competitors in OpenAI, which are trying to offer tokens at cheaper prices. You have folks like Microsoft, which offer your services, and yet are also trying to sell their own models. And they say oftentimes that some of those models, or at least some of the features of their models, can do some of the same things, maybe not at the frontier level. How do you think about that in terms of what that means longer term to the margins for the company?
DARIO AMODEI:  So, I think, I think a couple concepts. One concept is the frontier. And we have found that there are these incredible returns to the frontier. And in most products or goods, you have competition on price. Here, the competition is really on quality, because the returns to greater cognitive ability are so high, right? As we climb the exponential of cognitive ability, you go from doing chatbots, to being able to do coding, to being able to do biology and robotics. And the economic value of things further along the frontier is so much larger than things earlier in the frontier that that's where most of the value accumulates. The second idea is that, if you're good at the frontier, you are also good at producing smaller and more efficient models away from the frontier. So, if you look at Haiku 5.5, we were able to drop the price by 4X from Haiku 4.5 and by many times from Opus and Fable 5 family, which are, which it's, which it's much cheaper than. And so we are able to also compete using our, the same technology that we build our models, models on the frontier, the same compute multipliers, to make these cheap models that compete away from the frontier.

articles.title_orig: AMD sheds nearly $100 billion in market value as China chip concerns hit AI stocks
articles.title_zh: AMD sheds nearly $100 billion in market value as China chip concerns hit AI stocks
articles.content_orig:
Concerns about balance sheets and valuations in the artificial intelligence sector have hit the market hard since October, and investors who have shorted publicly traded tech companies in the AI trade have profited. Most investors don't think as much about "shorting" debt, but there will be a way through exchange-traded funds to profit from widening credit default swap spreads of top AI companies.
Both Tuttle Capital and Defiance ETFs have filed for funds that target the credit default swaps of companies closely linked to the AI trade, from CoreWeave and Oracle to the Magnificent Seven: Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms, Microsoft Corporation, Nvidia, Tesla, and Apple.
Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier. CDS is a closely watched indicator of issuer health in the debt markets, especially in the AI market this year. The ETFs are designed to gain when the CDS spreads of these companies widen, either as a group in the case of a Magnificent Seven CDS fund, or individually in the case of proposed ETFs targeting Oracle, CoreWeave and Meta. The funds would lose value when the market assesses the creditworthiness of these debt issuers as improving.
Both ETF managers filed for CoreWeave and Oracle CDS funds, specifically, among broader AI and semiconductor company CDS portfolios.
If the exchange-traded fund managers get approval from the Securities and Exchange Commission, these portfolios would be the first of their kind in an ETF market that has become more aggressive in recent years about launching higher-risk strategies revolving around more complex financial instruments than just public stocks and bonds. The ETF managers plan to employ leverage in the portfolios, which both increases risk and the potential for outsized returns on any given day, similar to the way existing single-stock leverage and inverse ETFs function.
The ETF managers say these CDS funds can serve an important role in a market on edge about AI debt.
"As AI infrastructure investment accelerates and companies take on significant capital commitments to fund that growth, we see an opportunity to give investors more targeted tools to manage credit risk and hedge potential financial stress across some of the biggest names driving the AI buildout," Sylvia Jablonski, CIO of Defiance ETFs, said in a statement to CNBC.
Neocloud companies like CoreWeave are a major focus for AI skeptics, an AI bubble watch compounded by the exit of Jensen Huang from Nvidia, who is seen as a critical player in financing the AI buildout, with Nvidia called by some the "central bank of AI ."
Apollo Global Management CEO Marc Rowan on Tuesday said that neocloud company AI projects could face an existential crisis if Nvidia funding dries up. "There was a strong incentive for Nvidia as a business matter to get these projects off the ground," Rowan said in an interview with CNBC's " Squawk on the Street ." "If that banking function, that guarantor function, gets taken away, access to capital for a large number of neoclouds is going to disappear."
In its earnings filings and conference call on Tuesday, Nvidia shifted the tone in discussing the way it finances the AI ecosystem.
Matthew Tuttle, founder and CEO of Tuttle Capital Management, said it is less likely that these ETFs will find an audience among retail investors than smaller institutional players.
"It may be a stretch for the average retail guy," he said, but he added that having managed leveraged and inverse ETFs, it is clear that many investors "get interested" when a particular asset is seeing outsized moves, as has been the case with AI company-linked CDS in 2026. "The stuff that moves a lot is the stuff that tends to generate the most interest," he said.
Both prospectuses stress that these funds are not designed to move inversely to the reference companies' stocks and can lose money while a company's shares decline. They also note these funds don't short bonds or bet directly against a company's stock, and to buy CDS protection, they pay premiums, which are a unique cost to the fund manager whether or not credit conditions worsen.
The CDS of these companies have been on the move in a major way as part of the AI trade over the past year.
CoreWeave's 9.75% bond due in 2031 is yielding close to 16%, while spreads on its five-year credit default swaps were recently between 1,100-1,200. Spreads over 1,000 are generally considered a sign of distress.
CoreWeave executives have taken their messaging about the debt public, with co-founder and chief strategy officer Brian Venturo posting on X.com on Wednesday that he had purchased $30 million in unsecured company bonds and was going to hold them until maturity in 2031. "I've never been more confident in CoreWeave," he wrote.
Oracle CDS contracts have moved up over the past year from below 80 to a current range above 300.
The CDS spreads on the biggest tech companies, including Amazon and Meta as examples, rose over 100% within the past year, as their free cash flow turned negative from spending heavily on AI. Even though the market is much less concerned about their balance sheets than that of the neoclouds, major tech company CDS spreads did hit five-year highs earlier this month.
Tuttle said that these ETFs, if approved, would be the "easiest" to use for smaller institutions and family offices that want CDS exposure and "are either too small to trade with the Goldmans of the world or lack the in-house expertise to trade CDS on their own."
"It is a different way to hedge the AI trade," Tuttle said.
ETF investing experts expressed skepticism about this approach and market reception. "I don't see much demand materializing for these types of products," said Nate Geraci, president of NovaDius Wealth Management. But he added it does make sense to target these ETFs "at retail investors who are seeing scary headlines around AI capex spending. Yet another way to speculate (gamble)," he said.
Todd Sohn, chief ETF strategist at Baird Strategas, said he foresees confusion with how these funds will work. "How many non-professionals know what CDS are?" he said.
Tuttle says it won't take billions in assets to make an ETF focused on AI CDS a minor financial success. "My criteria is I want to see a runway to $20 million, which is about our breakeven. I see it here. It doesn't mean it will happen, but I think we have a decent chance."
— CNBC's Michelle Fox contributed to this report

"There is no disruption to our services," according to the statement.

JPMorganChase said on Monday that it experienced technical issues that triggered online delays across several major U.S. banks. Chase blamed the outage on a "software bug."
There have been several recent tech outages across the nation that affected air travel, email and hotel reservations, and even slowed classified internal communications at the National Security Agency.
Top Trump administration officials continued this week to insist that there is no evidence that those outages were the result of cyberattacks.

articles.title_orig: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
articles.title_zh: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
articles.content_orig:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global powerbroker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. He made an appeal for regional harmony, saying: “Members of Apec are like passengers riding the same ship. To navigate the waves of the Pacific, we must unite as one and look out for each other.”
However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – with the US president calling the Russian his “friend”. The peace declaration said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

articles.title_orig: 'Come to Moscow,' Putin urges Europeans after Shenzhen summit
articles.title_zh: 'Come to Moscow,' Putin urges Europeans after Shenzhen summit
articles.content_orig:
President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that Russia will not negotiate with Ukraine on a limited ceasefire, citing a Ukrainian strike this week on a major bridge connecting Russia and Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Putin made the remarks to reporters in Russian after meeting with President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China. He said he had discussed the possibility of a ceasefire in certain areas of Ukraine, but would not move forward with negotiations after Ukraine's strike on the Kerch Bridge, according to the Russian state news agencies.
The 12-mile bridge, which Putin ceremonially opened himself in 2018, is hugely symbolic as it links the Russian mainland with Crimea — territory that Russian forces occupied about four years earlier. The missile strike this week wasn't the first time Ukraine had targeted the piece of infrastructure, but it inflicted severe damage. Russia also struck two major bridges in Kyiv the same day.
Putin played down the bridge's strategic importance on Thursday and said he had heard the calls "from all sides" for a naval ceasefire or a suspension of strikes on energy facilities, but he ruled out direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing the attack on the bridge.
"Honestly, I discussed the issue with my colleagues at the Security Council, and I asked them to think about it and go back to the issue, so that we could reach some agreements," Putin said, according to Russian state news agency TASS. "However, we will not make agreements after strikes on the Crimean Bridge. We will respond to these strikes."
Putin vowed that Russia's retaliation for the strike on the bridge would be severe, TASS reported.
While Putin claims frequently to want peace, he denies that Russia started the war with his order for a full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, and Russia's attacks on Ukraine have been relentless.
It's not clear how much Ukraine came up in Mr. Trump's one-on-one meeting with Putin on Wednesday, or in the meeting with both Putin and Xi on Thursday. Last week, the White House said Ukraine wouldn't be a topic of discussion, but before he left for Asia, Mr. Trump said the three leaders would be discussing the war. The White House readout of the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting was sparse on detail, and did not mention Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Mr. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff have been in Germany to meet with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and other European leaders about Ukraine and other topics.
Kushner said they discussed the "latest efforts to achieve a just, lasting and durable peace in Ukraine."
"We are grateful for his leadership, constructive engagement, and close partnership as we work together toward our shared goal of ending this terrible war and building a secure and prosperous future for Ukraine and Europe," Kushner posted to X .
Merz, speaking to reporters after the meeting, called the China summit a photo-op and said the trilateral format "will not bring peace" in Ukraine.
As he went to shake Putin's hand before an earlier meeting Wednesday on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China, Mr. Trump referred to the Russian leader as "my friend."
"Who is he?" the president said, pointing at Putin and smiling. "He's my friend."

articles.title_zh: Chinese tech firms fear AI hits from US curbs after Nvidia fallout
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Chinese technology firms are bracing for impacts on their ambitious artificial intelligence plans as the U.S. tightens restrictions on China 's access to the world's cutting-edge chips.
Chinese tech giant Alibaba , which on Thursday announced another quarter of strong revenue growth for its global AI cloud and compute services, warned that the new U.S. rules could affect some of its global data center expansion plans. It said it was still assessing the repercussions.
The Trump administration this week issued new rules in the wake of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, following the news that he’d had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
The rules now restrict remote computing access through data centers in third countries, the latest U.S. move to curtail China’s abilities to use advanced Nvidia chips to train its increasingly capable AI models.
Alibaba's AI revenues are surging as demand grows
As the technology race between the two superpowers intensifies, existing U.S. export restrictions already barred China from getting the world’s most powerful chips.
But some Chinese companies have been able to bypass those restrictions by renting remote computing access to train AI models, pushing the U.S. to close what some policymakers called a loophole.
As global AI usage grows, Alibaba has been expanding its capabilities across chips, cloud infrastructure and AI models. It launched its flagship Qwen4-Max AI model earlier this week. In September, Alibaba's CEO called its new Zhenwu V900 chip the “most powerful” AI chip in China, while it announced massive data center investment plans in China and abroad.
Alibaba Cloud’s AI-related revenue currently comes significantly from China and there’s still a lot of “untapped demand” from Chinese enterprises, said Jacob Cooke of the Beijing-based consultancy WPIC Marketing + Technologies.
For the latest July-September quarter, Alibaba reported a 53% year-on-year revenue surge for its AI cloud and compute services to nearly 61 billion yuan ($9 billion). Total revenue for the quarter rose 10% from the year before to almost 272 billion yuan ($41 billion), slightly better than what analysts had expected.
While the company has a strong cash buffer, capital expenditures jumped 60% during the quarter to 50.5 billion yuan ($7.6 billion) thanks to its increased spending on AI infrastructure buildout.
Tencent says US chip curb ‘sets everyone back in China’
Chinese tech giant Tencent on Wednesday said the new U.S. rule on chip access “sets everyone back in China.”
“Everyone is actually having less compute, advanced compute, to work with, no matter when you actually started leasing or building capacities outside of China,” Tencent President Martin Lau said on an earnings call. Training timelines for Tencent’s next versions of its AI models would probably be impacted, he said.
“Chinese AI firms are still heavily dependent on the most frontier Nvidia chips," said James Chai, a researcher at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, with new U.S. rules on remote access cutting off a huge portion of Chinese firms’ access to compute.
A study released in October by the Institute for Progress, a U.S. think tank, estimated that remote access to AI chips through overseas data centers could account for roughly one-third of China’s AI compute by the end of 2027.
Nvidia, meanwhile, said it is now “no longer shipping” chips including the H200, one of its more powerful chips, though not the most advanced, although the Trump administration greenlighted some sales to China, reflecting how Nvidia has toughened its stance on China following Huang’s ouster.
Analysts expect the U.S. will step up its chip export control policies against China after Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former senior executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, raised U.S. national security concerns. Earlier reporting by The New York Times suggested that U.S. officials suspected Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited in part to potentially influence Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available to Chinese companies.
Beijing has rejected claims that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, and has called the new U.S. rules blocking Chinese companies' remote access to computing power overseas “economic coercion.”
Analysts and industry leaders in China say the U.S.’s tightening of chip export control measures would ultimately accelerate China’s push to make its domestic chip industry self-sufficient.
“Over the longer run, we believe all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips, which we actually see the industry is actually progressing very fast,” said Tencent's Lau.

articles.title_orig: UK government forced to disclose secret Apple backdoor order
articles.title_zh: UK government forced to disclose secret Apple backdoor order
articles.content_orig:
A British tribunal has confirmed that the UK government ordered Apple Inc. to provide a means of accessing encrypted customer information, delivering a significant transparency ruling in a dispute that has raised concerns about digital privacy, government surveillance and the security of consumer technology.
The Investigatory Powers Tribunal ruled Thursday that British authorities had failed to demonstrate that publicly acknowledging the order would jeopardize national security, according to Reuters .
The decision marks a setback for the government’s efforts to keep its surveillance demands confidential, although it does not determine whether Apple must comply with the underlying request.
At the center of the dispute is a technical capability notice, a legal mechanism through which British authorities can require technology companies to facilitate access to information for lawful investigations.
The government had maintained that it could neither verify nor deny issuing such a notice, arguing that disclosure could compromise intelligence operations and assist potential adversaries.
The tribunal rejected that position, concluding that extensive media coverage and previous public statements had already revealed enough information about the dispute that official acknowledgment would cause little additional harm, Reuters reported.
The legal confrontation follows a series of British government efforts to obtain access to information protected by Apple’s encryption technology.
In January 2025, UK authorities issued an initial demand seeking a way to access encrypted cloud backups belonging to customers in Britain and the United States, according to Reuters.
That request prompted diplomatic discussions with President Donald Trump’s administration, which ultimately resulted in the British government withdrawing the original demand.
The dispute resurfaced in July 2026, when British authorities issued another notice focused specifically on Apple’s UK customers.
Apple subsequently renewed its legal challenge before the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, a specialist judicial body responsible for reviewing complaints involving surveillance and intelligence powers.
The company’s ability to publicly explain its objections has been constrained by legal confidentiality requirements surrounding the government’s demands.
The confrontation highlights the competing priorities facing technology companies and national security authorities. Governments argue that access to digital evidence can be essential to criminal investigations, while encryption providers warn that deliberately weakening security protections could expose customers to additional risks.
Related: Data Portability’s Cybersecurity Paradox: When Protecting Consumer Data Restricts Competition
Apple has previously argued that creating a mechanism for government access to encrypted information could also create vulnerabilities exploitable by cybercriminals or hostile governments, according to earlier Reuters reporting.
Civil liberties organizations Liberty and Privacy International challenged the government’s refusal to acknowledge the notice, arguing that the secrecy prevented meaningful public scrutiny of surveillance powers.
During proceedings in September, lawyers representing the organizations and Apple criticized the government’s confidentiality position as incompatible with principles of open justice, Reuters reported.
The tribunal’s decision gives privacy advocates an important procedural victory by establishing that the government cannot automatically rely on national security concerns to conceal the existence of the order.
Liberty welcomed the outcome as a victory for transparency.
Akiko Hart, the organization’s director, said the public should be informed when government decisions have consequences for privacy and security, according to Reuters.
The ruling also addressed arguments that disclosing the notice could provide useful intelligence to hostile actors. The tribunal found those concerns insufficient to justify continued secrecy about the order’s existence, given the information already publicly available.
The court referred to previous reporting by British newspapers, including The Times and the Financial Times, in assessing how widely the government’s actions had already become known.
Thursday’s decision concerns the public acknowledgment of the notice rather than its legality or enforceability.
A substantive hearing examining Apple’s challenge is not expected until 2027, according to Reuters.
The tribunal also indicated that certain related decisions would remain confidential because releasing them could harm the public interest. Questions about how much additional information concerning the government’s demands can be disclosed will be considered separately.
Neither Apple nor the British government had provided an immediate response to the ruling at the time of Reuters’ initial report.

articles.title_orig: ‘I came close to killing Sally about six times’: how my abusive father was enabled by his fame
articles.title_zh: ‘I came close to killing Sally about six times’: how my abusive father was enabled by his fame
articles.content_orig:
Like Russell Brand, my father was put on a pedestal by the media, despite a history of troubling, misogynistic comments. Meanwhile, my mother suffered through years of appalling treatment
Even though decades have passed, part of me feels I should not be telling this story. Not because it isn’t true, but because telling makes it real. And the reality is very hard to bear.
I was a young child at home in Whitechapel, east London, when my mother came into my bedroom, which was next to my parents’, and told me that my father had raped her. He had gone off to work and I was too young to fully understand what the words meant – perhaps seven or eight – and I remember being angry with her for upsetting life again, as she had done before, when she suddenly came to me at the top of the stairs and told me that they would “have to part” and that would mean taking me away with her.
I couldn’t understand why life couldn’t just be nice in our house, a brick terrace with a handsome exterior, shabby inside and a crack through the stone of the front steps. Down in the dark basement and back yard, my mother had painted spectacular murals of exotic jungles and savannah filled with giraffes, elephants, leopards, tigers, hummingbirds, eagles and tree frogs.
I had my books and teddies and crafting station, and in photos it looks like I was filled with my mother’s joy and hope and creativity and happiness. But even if I didn’t have words for it at the time, my body did. I was tense from lack of sleep and bit my nails so relentlessly that my fingers are still bent. I couldn’t bear to be separated from my mother, following her around the house and refusing even to be left at nursery.
The love for my father that I felt when he told me scary stories, took me down to Brick Lane market, rescued old bikes from the canal, or lifted me up so that I could “walk on the ceiling” in the kitchen began to morph into something deeply uncomfortable, a feeling of the frightening tension between how you want things to be and how they have turned out. This came back to me with the trial of Russell Brand . Both he and my father did terrible things when no one was watching – and both were celebrated by the media. Looking back now, if I could have any wish granted, I’d see my father jailed for life.
Or maybe I’d just tell my mother to run and never look back. But it’s too late for that. She died in 2000, when I was 24, but in effect the death came much earlier.
It was around 1973 when Sally Hill, a bright 23-year-old final year student at Camberwell art school in London, first met my father, Brian, who was 47 and a friend of a member of staff. The younger brother of the famous writer, Brendan Behan, he was just starting work as a lecturer in media and general studies at the London College of Printing, having recently graduated from the University of Sussex and done a teacher training course. Prior to meeting my father, my mother had been dating a much younger man called Terry Scott, a boxer who unfortunately also knew my father and his first family, who were living on a houseboat in Shoreham in West Sussex. Terry took Sally down to visit and it wasn’t long before my mother was living on the boat too.
Having been discharged from the Irish army, my father had originally arrived in England with nothing and worked on building sites, quickly marrying his first wife, the daughter of his Communist landlord, when she was 16 and he was 24. After having three daughters with her, he had transitioned out of trade unionism and into teaching, despite a criminal record that included a six-week spell in prison for using threatening behaviour and insulting words to police during a strike.
According to one of his friends, he was unhappy before he met my mother and seemed markedly better afterwards. While he may have thought he loved my mother, calling her “the most beautiful woman I’ve ever seen”, it didn’t take long for his fanatically deep-seated sense of resentment to set in, especially once she started to argue with him about his unreasonable demands and lack of support. He claimed to hate traditional family structures, yet seemed to see her as his possession, to the extent that she soon found herself being held responsible for his erratic moods or anything that went wrong. Any challenge would result in a barrage of verbal, psychological and physical abuse.
This was not and would never be a fair or mutual relationship. She was not allowed to work because he was afraid she’d meet someone else, and despite her huge talent for painting, drawing and sculpture, these activities began to dwindle as his behaviour escalated after my birth in 1976.
My mother’s skills were perceived as a threat, and instead of celebrating her, my father rarely mentioned her, except to his close friends. Although he earned a good salary and we benefited from cheap lodging thanks to my maternal grandmother, who got the house through her job in the NHS, he got her to claim benefits as a “single mother”. Then he used this against her by threatening to report her if he needed to get his way.
My mother never had a bank account, and later, when we moved to Brighton, my father would list her in his tally of weekly spending, giving her cash and then berating her for spending too much on cigarettes. On her death certificate he registered her occupation as “Housewife – Wife of Brian Desmond Behan Playwright”.
In 1979, he published his first, deeply unpleasant, novel Time to Go, an unsuccessful book about a violent, misogynistic man named O’Brien who feels trapped by marriage and resolves to go after a young woman named Jeannie. O’Brien woos her with lies, “love bombing” her (“Say I can see you or I’ll die. I mean it, I will die”), while concealing his “growing contempt” for women in general. But, of course, he wants their bodies: “He felt he would do anything from rape, sodomy, exposure, child molestation, lies, anything to get a feel of another woman.”
Describing himself as “the most jealous and insecure man on earth”, O’Brien goes on: “Many of their rows were the result of his nasty mind calculating times of outings, times of coming in at night, where she had been and whom she had seen. His secret desire to lock her up was just part of his desire to dominate her.”
Everything I have come to know about my father tells me this was a thinly veiled account of his own life and attitudes. My mother may have come to the same conclusion, but by the time he exposed himself in print, she was pregnant with my brother and her fate was sealed. Although she appeared strong to most people outside the family, the ambitious, happy-go-lucky free spirit went into retreat. In its place came a woman who created a tough front to push through the days, but behind it she was withdrawn, sad, confused and increasingly depressed, using alcohol to numb herself.
Meanwhile, my father was using the standard tactics of a skilled perpetrator, undermining her sense of self to the point that she questioned her own reality. He would tell her that things didn’t happen when they did, that she was exaggerating, or, when things really escalated, that no one would believe her because he had friends in the media and she was nothing, would never be anything.
A s well as a gifted artist who taught me painting, screen printing, lino cutting, pottery, marbling, mask-making and candle making, Sally was a fantastic vegetarian cook, and decades ahead of her time in her understanding of the environment, health and educational theory. And she was, of course, a wonderful mother. Yet he was the one with the talent, he told her.
At some point, we got used to the dichotomy of a rich life filled with creativity and its horrible, almost unreal contrast. What is most devastating about domestic abusers is that they expertly tread the line of plausible deniability, so my father always had an excuse or “provocation” for his misdeeds. And since the bad was mixed with good, there was always the hope that ne

Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices were down about 7% Wednesday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."
Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.
The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."
CNBC did not independently verify this information.
Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."
The allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.
AMD did not immediately reply to a CNBC request for comment.
Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, said on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.

articles.title_orig: Vladimir Putin invites European leaders to Moscow
articles.title_zh: Vladimir Putin invites European leaders to Moscow
articles.content_orig:
BRUSSELS ― After the EU and its allies wrestled over who should represent them in talks over Ukraine, they now face an even harder decision: play hardball with Russia or try a subtler approach?
The challenge of agreeing on red lines, or principles, for the European team in any negotiations is already proving divisive, with the EU’s chief diplomat Kaja Kallas saying the Europeans should start by demanding as much as possible, and some governments, such as Austria, advocating a looser approach, including confidence-building measures.
“There’s a range of things that Europe should make clear that it’s not ready to discuss,” Norway’s Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide said.
Europe was largely left out of talks between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. in Abu Dhabi last week, but the Kremlin and the White House signaled that wouldn’t be the case at future meetings. After days of disagreement, EU leaders settled on a team made up of officials from four major countries ― France, Germany, Italy and Poland ― plus the U.K. and top representatives from NATO and the European Commission and Council.
Now, “the focus must shift from the ‘who’ to the ‘what’,” Austrian Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger said.
In a 15-point paper shared ahead of a foreign ministers’ meeting on Monday, Austria spelled out what some of those confidence-building measures could be: proposing limited or partial ceasefires to pave the way for a wider truce, for instance, or offering to set up an international forum to monitor any peace agreement.
The proposal amounts to “an offer to all 27 [EU countries] to work towards a common position,” Meinl-Reisinger said.
Norway, which isn’t part of Europe’s negotiating team but had direct contacts with Russia, is also floating ideas to lower tensions. Ukraine’s backers should look back to the Cold War for examples of how Russia and the West managed extreme tensions, specifically the 1975 “Helsinki Accords” which laid out principles for state-to-state relations, Foreign Minister Barth Eide said.
“NATO deployments in NATO countries, for instance, is not a question to discuss with Russia” but Cold War deals on arms limitation “must be relevant in the post-war scenario.”
In the same vein, officials close to the talks are calling for a “flexible” mandate that would allow participants to actually negotiate, rather than have their hands tied. The job of drafting the mandate must go to EU ambassadors in their Coreper meetings, not foreign ministers, argued two EU officials.
Further complicating the matter, such a mandate would bind the European representatives at the table ― the Commission’s Bjoern Seibert, the European Council’s Anna-Maria Boura and the advisers from France, Poland, Italy and Germany ― but not those from the U.K. or NATO.
For Kallas, however, it should be the foreign ministers she gathers in Brussels each month who draft the mandate — and as far as she’s concerned, the approach should demand up-front concessions from Russia rather than the other way around.
“The foreign ministers are ready to take this work forward,” she told reporters on Monday, pointing out that she had already suggested a list of demands .
“I was a lawyer,” she said. “How do you enter negotiations? First, you present or prepare the absolute maximum you want to see. Then, not openly, you also prepare where you are ready to … step back to and what are your red lines, which are absolute no-gos.”
Ministers from several Baltic, Nordic and eastern flank countries echoed Kallas’s approach.
“We have to really keep sequencing, and it means that we have to agree on the ceasefire and when the guns go silent, then we negotiate on the long-lasting peace on Ukraine,” Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said.
Estonia’s chief envoy, Margus Tsahkna, echoed the point: “First, Putin can start the ceasefire. Then negotiations between Russia and Ukraine about peace, and if the peace is there, we need to discuss what kind of security guarantees will be given to Ukraine. We also need Ukrainian security guarantees to our region.”
The only problem is that Europe has already effectively conceded that talks will continue even without a ceasefire. EU negotiators see talks resuming in the coming weeks in Abu Dhabi and are banking on being in the room with Russia’s representatives, according to two EU officials, despite the fact that Moscow is carrying out daily attacks across Ukraine.
“It’s about being pragmatic,” said a senior EU official, granted anonymity to speak frankly. “The people in the room must be able to make decisions.”

articles.title_orig: The Best ‘GTA 6’ Gun Is Very Easy To Get From The Start
articles.title_zh: The Best ‘GTA 6’ Gun Is Very Easy To Get From The Start
articles.content_orig:
After a 13-year wait and endless memes, the time has come for gamers of all stripes to call out of work for a few days and put their noses to the Grand Theft Auto grindstone. To put this in perspective, when "Grand Theft Auto 5" came out, the Tesla Model S was the best EV you could get had a range of 265 miles. Today, the longest-range EV SUVs are pushing past 400 miles. Before you put your headphones on and play for four days straight without coming up for air, though, there's something important you should know about how Rockstar's newest game works.
Car trunks are an integral component of how you'll plan missions and play the game. Why? Turns out, they're your best tool for managing inventory while on the go. Unlike in "Grand Theft Auto 5," where you had a functionally limitless inventory and could whip out your RPG on a dime and start blasting, it's looking like inventory management is going to be a big part of the gameplay in "Grand Theft Auto 6." You start the game with a set amount of stuff you can carry on your character, whether it's Lucia or Jason, and there's no way to increase that amount over the course of the game.
That's right. There's no raising skills or buying a larger carrying capacity, like in "Cyberpunk 2077." No trading Korok seeds for more slots, like in "Breath of the Wild." And certainly no princess treatment like an infinite inventory. What you see is what you get, and what you take into a mission is all you have. Thankfully, you can stuff a limited amount of gear into your ride's rear, allowing you a little extra flexibility while out exploring Vice City in your unlicensed, legally distinct Mercedes-Benz .
Taking full advantage of your trunk's inventory is mercifully easy. You just have to find where you parked your car (you parked in a designated space, right?) and open up your trunk, just like you would in real life. You can swap out gear you're carrying with gear stashed in the trunk, or you can keep your trunk empty, unload loot into it, and get back out to where the action is with inventory slots open for further finds.
If, for some reason, you decide to commit crimes while out enjoying a drive, you can clean up your mess by stuffing bodies in the trunk, too. You wouldn't do that, though, because you're a law-abiding citizen of Vice City, not a crazed criminal stealing cars and engaging in pointless police chases .
Your usable trunk isn't just handy for extra inventory, though. It could save your skin while evading the cops. Police in "Grand Theft Auto 6" are smarter than they've ever been (in-game, not in real life, obviously). When you get into trouble with the law, police NPCs will track certain characteristics of Jason and Lucia, which helps track these criminals across the city. They'll remember details like what clothes you're wearing, what weapons you're wielding, and what car you're driving.
You'll want to carry extra weapons and a change of clothes in your extra trunk storage. That way, when you get into trouble, you can run back to your car, complete a magical-girl transformation into your new outfit, and lower the likelihood that you'll get caught. Be careful, though. GTA 6 has Flock-like cameras that track your character's movements , and you'll have to stop at gas stations to fuel up virtually . So much for gaming being a break from reality.
GTA 6's usable trunk system promises to make the gameplay more dynamic and more challenging in fun ways, and it's a big departure from what franchise fans will be used to from "Grand Theft Auto 4" and "Grand Theft Auto 5." However, this isn't a completely original idea.
In fact, this is actually a reprise of a similar mechanic from an earlier Rockstar game. "L.A. Noire" is a 2011 neo-noir mystery game that also used a storage system that involved the trunk of the player character's car. Like GTA, "L.A. Noire" also features plenty of car chases and guns, though you play as a detective named Cole Phelps and try to solve crimes rather than commit them.
You may also remember a similar mechanic from the critically acclaimed and award-winning 2018 game "Red Dead Redemption 2." In "Red Dead Redemption 2," main character Arthur Morgan keeps a saddle on his horse that functions as additional storage. Much like in "Grand Theft Auto 6," returning to your horse allowed you to dig through your saddlebags and pull out both weapons and clothes, which are used to evade enemies and equip the different outfits needed for different weather.
For better or worse, inventory management is frequently one of the stickiest parts of game design, and it can make or break a game. Let's all cross our fingers extra hard that "Grand Theft Auto 6" nails the trunk storage mechanics and that changing your clothes in your car isn't a total drag like it is in real life.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine strikes Putin’s prized Crimean bridge for third time in a week
articles.title_zh: Ukraine strikes Putin’s prized Crimean bridge for third time in a week
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine struck the bridge linking Russia and Crimea for the third time in a week, forcing a suspension of train services across it, Russian authorities said, hours before President Vladimir Putin met the leaders of China and the U.S.
The timing and impact of Ukraine‘s attacks on the bridge, the longest in Europe and a symbol of Putin’s Russia, are awkward for the Kremlin chief as he participates in what Moscow has cast as a historic trilateral summit with President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping .
Moscow hopes the meeting will send a signal to allies and foes that it — rather than the European Union and Britain — is part of an emerging new multilateral world order.
There was no immediate comment on the latest attack from Ukraine or Volodymyr Zelenskyy , its president, who was due to hold talks in Berlin later on Thursday with U.S. peace envoys.
Sergei Aksyonov, Crimea’s Russian-installed governor, issued a defiant video message in which he said rail travel across the bridge would resume later on Thursday.
“We have the strength, the resolve and the understanding of how to resolve this situation. We will overcome everything. Crimea is with Russia forever!” Aksyonov said.
In a statement, Russia’s transport ministry said that nobody had been hurt in the latest Ukrainian attack on the Black Sea peninsula, which Moscow annexed from Ukraine in 2014 , and that specialists were assessing damage to the bridge.
The 12-mile bridge is a flagship project that Putin inaugurated in 2018 and that symbolizes Russia’s attachment to the peninsula, which is also the home of its Black Sea Fleet, whose ships Ukraine has repeatedly targeted.
On Tuesday, Ukrainian drones and missiles destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, forcing its main road arch to crumble into the sea while leaving a yawning gap, according to videos and images verified by Reuters, dealing a military and symbolic blow to Russia.
That attack is likely to make it harder for Russia to keep up supplies to the peninsula, which is home to nearly 2.5 million people, and is likely to put pressure on Russian military logistics in parts of southern Ukraine held by Moscow’s forces.
This week‘s first attack, on Monday, caused more minor damage to the bridge.

articles.title_orig: The Best Ways To Earn Money In ‘GTA 6,’ Early, Mid- And Late-Game
articles.title_zh: The Best Ways To Earn Money In ‘GTA 6,’ Early, Mid- And Late-Game
articles.content_orig:
Get unlimited access to everything VICE has to offer.
Money can be tight at the start of Grand Theft Auto VI , especially when you need cash to progress the story. Here’s how to make money fast in GTA 6 , including where to find your first Illegal Operation and when you can start selling parked cars.
The fastest way to make money in GTA 6 Chapters 1 and 2 is to steal narcotics from Illegal Operations and sell them to Brian or Donnie in Chapter 1, or Dunk in Chapter 2. You can also sell stolen cars for quick cash or go treasure diving with Kenton for a payout later in the Grand Theft Auto VI’s story .
In Chapter 1, Key Lento has one main Illegal Operation called Exotic Animals Front . You can also access two Kingfisher Illegal Operations in the swamps to the northwest, Fishing Shacks and Manatee Hotel .
To get into Exotic Animals Front, find the Three Sheets Liquor store in the middle of Key Lento. From the front of the store, head around the right side of the building and wrap around until you are on the backside of it.
You will eventually find a hole in the wall you can climb through. Take out the three enemies inside, then head into the back room.
Once inside of the Exotic Animals Front backroom, there’s a safe you can break open for cash without a code.
After you reach Port Gellhorn in Chapter 2, La Cascara Motel is one of the best Illegal Operations for earning money. For the fastest payout in either chapter, grab any narcotics you find during these operations and sell them to Brian or Donnie in Chapter 1 or Bunk in Chapter 2 .
Make sure to check out our guide on All GTA 6 Safe Codes in Chapter 2 to make even more money quickly.
In Chapter 1, you can steal cars driving down the street and sell them at any Pay and Spray . There’s a limit to how many cars you can sell there every 24 in-game hours, so it’s a good way to earn some extra cash between Illegal Operations.
In Chapter 2, befriending Moses unlocks the ability to “Jimmy” open parked cars. Moses also has no daily limit on how many cars you can sell him, making this a more reliable way to earn money once you reach Port Gellhorn.
Visiting Kenton in Key Lento unlocks treasure hunting. You’ll get access to his boat and a scanner you can use to locate sunken treasure while diving.
Tracking down the treasure can take a while, and Kenton only pays you after he sells the valuables. That can take a few hours after you hand them over.
The payout is sizable once it comes through, so this is worth doing while you progress the story if you already have enough cash for your next mission. Overall these are the best methods to make money fast in GTA 6’s early chapters .
Although in Chapter 2 you will eventually unlock the ability to rob stores, including gas stations and jewelry stores. However, this is tied to main story progression.

articles.title_orig: Pebble Index 01 AI Ring Review: When A Single Feature Becomes The Product
articles.title_zh: Pebble Index 01 AI Ring Review: When A Single Feature Becomes The Product
articles.content_orig:
It’s a whimsical side project for the smartwatch company, but a useful one.
In 2009, Apple CEO Steve Jobs met with the founders of Dropbox with the intention of buying the file-sharing service. As part of the negotiation, Jobs reportedly said Dropbox was a "feature, not a product," and the business couldn't survive long term in its own right. That was my first thought when Pebble CEO Eric Migicovsky showed me the Index 01 back in January. A $75 non-smart ring that puts a tiny microphone on your finger just for speaking to your AI!? Surely, that's a (software) feature on a watch or smart ring, not a whole product you could sell in its own right. All I can say is that I'm glad I didn't say those words out loud at the time, because I'd be eating them today.
The Index 01 is the first of what Migicovsky hopes will be many small, slightly whimsical side projects made by the revived Pebble. It's a non-smart, stainless steel ring which sits on your index finger with a single physical rubber-clad button and an RGB LED.
Inside, you'll find a short range microphone, Bluetooth and a non-rechargeable silver oxide battery. As the rings are sold for $75, and it's designed to be used in tiny bursts, that cell is expected to last between two and three years. When the battery is close to running out, you'll get a ping from Pebble asking if you want to buy a replacement. At that point, you'll also be asked to send back your existing ring for recycling, since Pebble doesn't want to be making more e-waste. A gold star for everyone who can spot the contradiction there.
You'll be able to pick up the Index 01 in US sizes 6-13, and there's a waitlist where you can sign up if you want one in sizes 14 or 15. Pebble says that it's water resistant to one meter, withstanding handwashing, showers and doing the dishes, but it's best not to swim with it.
If you don't know your ring size and don't feel like taking a risk, you can grab a sizing kit from the company. You'll get an injection-molded set of sizers back for you to wear for a day or two to check the fit, and I'd urge you to keep a craft knife or pair of sprue cutters on hand.
As I said, the idea here is to put a physical talk to your device button on your index finger for the thoughts you just need to dump out of your mental cache. By default, if you hold the button and talk, your words will be sent to its homegrown AI, Index Agent, but you can also set it to be processed locally. The button has a wonderfully satisfying click, which is both great to feel and means there's so much resistance that I've only accidentally activated it once in my time wearing it. When active, you need to hold the ring less than a foot away from your mouth to issue your edict (any further is probably physically impossible anyway), and within about 10 seconds it'll be processed on your phone.
Plenty of the things that the Index 01 is doing is the sort of bread-and-butter ambient computing that's been knocking around for years. With your voice, you can leave yourself notes and reminders, add items to a shopping list or set timers, with the system working out where to place each one. There are separate panes inside the Pebble app for Notes to Self, Reminders and Shopping List, which has worked flawlessly so far, even with oblique requests.
You can, of course, also ask Index Agent to answer questions about your schedule and to pull information from the internet. I found the former to be much more reliable than the latter, and the agent managed to embarrass itself in at least one of my tests. One of my usual go-tos is to ask agents who the current manager of a soccer team is, given the volatility of such a role. During testing, Mauricio Pochettino stepped down as the manager of the US men's national team to take over a team sitting in the bottom three of the Premier League. When I asked Index who was running the US men's team, it suggested Pochettino — no great shame in not being that up to date. But, when I asked who was managing the club he was about to take over, it said Ruben Amorim, who was fired January 5, 2026 and has had two successors since then.
Now, I'm the sort of person who doesn't use ambient computing because, for me, I don't like the privacy implications of having a device which is always listening. Equally important, I know I can do whatever task I need with my fingers faster than I could render it as speech. I can set a kitchen timer on my phone in about five seconds, saying it out loud takes twice as long. But the fact Index 01 is only listening when I activate it, and that it's on my finger already, flips the script.
Inside the Pebble app, you can change the destination to whatever AI agent you use, and also change what the trigger action. So, for instance, if you'd rather trigger a web search or a webhook, you can do that, as well as hook up to an MCP server. As I said when reviewing the Pebble Time 2 , the app lacks polish, as the focus is on adding functionality over gloss. And I think the target market — people who didn't just have to look up what a webhook / MCP server was — won't be deterred.
Pebble is an Android-first company, and the ring can do several more things when paired with that ecosystem over iOS. Double click the ring and you'll trigger music playback, a triple click advances to the next song and you can set the ring to send messages via Beeper.
As usual, Pebble has made the point that there are plenty of other devices available if you want something outside its narrow offering. In its materials, the company says if you want a smart ring get an Oura ($399) and if you want a long-term AI recorder, get a Plaud. (The Plaud NotePin is $159, which can continuously record up to 20 hours of audio for later transcription.)
In terms of similar devices, the most obvious choice is the Wizpr Ring , which I saw at CES 2024 when it was called the Whsp Ring . The company is currently fulfilling Indiegogo orders, where rings were priced at $139, but says its retail price will be $199 when it launches. Vocci's ring will set you back $299, can record up to eight hours of conversations at a time and will let you speak to your AI agents. Just bear in mind, it comes with a monthly subscription which will only offer up unlimited transcription at the $30 a month tier. Another option is Aina's far fancier ring , which was announced at the start of November and will ship early next year for $399.
The Pebble Index 01 is nothing more than a physical manifestation of what would otherwise be a software feature. A discrete, standalone button that I'd argue nobody really needs , but it's useful enough to easily justify if you want one. I'm not going to try and dissuade you if your initial reaction was much like mine, because it's the sane and sensible thing to think. But bear in mind that, at this sort of price, it's the type of low-investment gadget that might wind up finding itself an integral part of far more people's days than anyone expects.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive: Here’s the Motorola Razr Flex, a Wide Rival to the Galaxy Z Fold 8
articles.title_zh: Exclusive: Here’s the Motorola Razr Flex, a Wide Rival to the Galaxy Z Fold 8
articles.content_orig:
SammyGuru is reader-supported. We have affiliate and sponsored partnerships, so we may earn a commission when you buy through links on our site, at no extra cost to you. Posts may contain sponsored or affiliate link placements. Learn more .
Samsung went wide with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 this year, and Motorola is getting ready to answer with a wide foldable of its own. Until now, the Razr Flex had only shown up in leaked specs, mockups, and a live photo posted on Reddit . Today you can get a much better look. SammyGuru can now show you exclusive imagery of the Motorola Razr Flex, the company’s first wide book-style Razr, in green and beige.
The Razr Flex opens like a book, just like the Fold 8, and its main screen is wide enough to feel more like a small tablet than a tall phone. Closed, it works like a regular phone, with a punch-hole selfie camera centered at the top of the cover screen. The inner display has its own punch-hole camera in the corner.
Around the back, a pill-shaped camera bar holds two cameras and a flash, with Motorola’s logo in the middle and the Razr name near the bottom. The hinge also lets the phone stand on its own half-open, so you can prop it up on a table and use it hands-free.
Smartwatch of your choice, up to $499
Earlier reports named the two colors PANTONE Dark Botanical Garden and PANTONE Coriander, and here are both. The green version pairs a woven, fabric-like back with a matching green frame. The beige version gets a pebbled, leather-like back and a champagne frame.
Leaks so far point to a smaller and cheaper phone than Samsung’s. Earlier reports put the Razr Flex’s main screen at about 6.9 inches and its cover screen at about 5 inches. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 has a 7.6-inch main display and a 5.5-inch cover screen. The Razr Flex is also rumored to cost around $1,700 in the US, about $200 less than the Fold 8’s $1,899 starting price.
Like the Fold 8, which pairs two 50MP cameras with no telephoto, the Razr Flex appears to stick with two rear cameras. If the size and price rumors hold, Motorola’s pitch looks clear: a wide foldable for people who found the Fold 8 too big or too expensive.
Motorola hasn’t announced the Razr Flex or said when it will go on sale. A test version of Motorola’s Australian support site listed the phone and hinted at a 2027 debut, and Motorola launched the Razr Fold at CES in January. We’ll update this story as soon as Motorola makes the Razr Flex official.
Would you pick a smaller, cheaper wide foldable over the Galaxy Z Fold 8?

articles.title_orig: Where To Get The Car Key Cloner In ‘GTA 6’
articles.title_zh: Where To Get The Car Key Cloner In ‘GTA 6’
articles.content_orig:
It wouldn’t be Grand Theft Auto without some grand theft auto, but the way the system works now in GTA 6 takes a little understanding, and in some ways, may frustrate players toward the beginning of the game. But here’s how it works, and when the elusive Key Cloner is going to hit your inventory, opening up better and better cars.
It’s been well-established at this point that GTA 6 has a tiered crime system, where you start out small-time and get better jobs with better rewards in time. That also applies to cars, and there are three tiers here.
Well, technically, the one you start with is like a tier 0, where you simply have to rip people out of cars or smash windows and set off alarms. But pretty quickly, as you go through the main story, you will meet a chop shop owner, Moses, who will give you the Slim Jim that lets you open up cars with no alarms; then you have to hotwire them.
This lasts a very long time. You will see nicer cars that command a higher sell price, but you cannot steal or sell them. All of them have a security system called a Key Cloner, meaning your Slim Jim won’t work, and even if you boot someone out of their already moving car, you cannot drive it without a Key Cloner.
You have to get a decent way into the story in order to get a Key Cloner. Minor spoilers follow. Eventually, once you make your way east toward Vice City itself, you will progress through the story and meet a second car-stealing connection, Randy. He has a list of rare cars he wants stolen, but as you start the list, he will give you the fabled Key Cloner.
Great news! But there’s a big caveat. You will now notice that there are two tiers of trackers on Key Cloned cars, Standard and Advanced. Randy, and soon Pay-n-Sprays, will only take cars with Standard Trackers. A Standard Tracker doesn’t really do anything, but it limits the tier of car you can get. Advanced trackers apply to most Ferrari/Lamborghini equivalent supercars you will see on the map, or ultra-luxury vehicles like Bentley/Rolls Royce types.
The Advanced Tracker gets crazy. If you slow down for too long in these cars, you will automatically give the cops your location and have to run to escape them each time. This could be slowing down for a turn or, god forbid, getting in a crash. The other problem is that for a very, very long time, you will not actually be able to do anything with these cars. You cannot sell or register them with Randy or Pay-n-Spray as they will not deal with Advanced Trackers. Rather, you have to get a whole lot of cars on Randy’s list turned in (he will pay you for those specific ones, once) and eventually finish out his storyline. Then he will agree to take those Advanced Tracker cars.
My advice? Sure, register the Advanced Tracker supercars you want once you can, if you can afford it, but if you are trying to steal cars for cash, don’t bother with them. Yes, almost all will have higher sell prices than Standard Tracker cars, but it is not worth dealing with the hassle of the cops being on you half the time. Standard Tracker cars can be $4-6 thousand to sell, and it’s a breeze to turn them in. Don’t bother with Advanced for a couple grand more. Enjoy the hunt.

articles.title_orig: Thanksgiving dinner will come with higher price tag: Research
articles.title_zh: Thanksgiving dinner will come with higher price tag: Research
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
Record turkey prices and higher fuel costs could make Thanksgiving dinner more expensive this year, according to a survey released Wednesday.
The American Farm Bureau Federation said the cost of an average Thanksgiving feast for 10 will rise 6% from last year to $58.63. The group tracks grocery prices using hundreds of volunteers in all 50 states and Puerto Rico.
The Farm Bureau, which has been tracking Thanksgiving costs for 40 years, said it’s the first time since 2022 that Americans will see the price of the meal increase. The price hit a record of $64.05 in 2022.
High diesel prices have made it more expensive for farmers to process and transport Thanksgiving staples like milk, dinner rolls, potatoes and cranberries, the Farm Bureau said. Diesel prices have surged since the start of the Iran war and hit a record average of $6.53 per gallon in the U.S. in September, according to AAA.
On Wednesday diesel averaged $5.96 per gallon, up 58% from a year ago, AAA said.
Turkey prices have also risen sharply over the past year. The Farm Bureau said the 16-pound turkey in its survey cost an average of $23.68 this year, up from $21.50 last year.
Bird flu has been decimating U.S. turkey flocks since an outbreak began in 2022. But cases have been waning, and turkey production increased substantially this year, said Mark Jordan, the executive director of Leap Market Analytics.
At the same time, turkey demand has been rising, as more Americans seek out lean protein and U.S. turkey exports rise. That strong demand has limited U.S. turkey inventories and raised prices. The U.S. Department of Agriculture expects the wholesale price of a whole frozen turkey hen will average a record $1.76 per pound this year, up 29% from last year.
“Over the last few years there’s been a lot of doom and gloom for the turkey industry,” Jordan said. “This is one of those years that turkey producers are feeling a little bit better about their lot in life.”
Jordan said diesel costs likely didn’t impact turkey prices this year, since so much of the decision-making and timing related to the turkeys that will be consumed this Thanksgiving happened before diesel prices spiraled. But diesel costs could have a notable impact on turkey prices next year, he said.
A few of the items on the Thanksgiving menu are cheaper than last year, the Farm Bureau said. A 1-pound vegetable tray featuring carrots and celery is 5 cents cheaper, while a 16-ounce bag of frozen peas is 4 cents cheaper. Frozen pie crusts are also slightly cheaper, although a can of pumpkin pie filling is more expensive.
And in some cases, stores will price turkey and other Thanksgiving staples lower in order to draw shoppers. Aldi said its feast for 10, which mirrors the Farm Bureau’s menu, costs $39 this year. Walmart, which adds items like corn muffin mix and marshmallows but doesn’t include carrots and celery, said its feast for 10 is $35.
Persistently high grocery prices have been frustrating Americans since the pandemic and played a role in Republicans’ recent losses in the midterm elections. Prices for food eaten at home jumped 22% between October 2021 and October 2026, according to U.S. government data. That’s almost double the usual pace of food price inflation.
This year, the USDA predicts prices for food eaten at home to rise 2.3%. That would be lower than the recent annual average of 2.6%.
Durbin writes for the Associated Press.
